content.text: The equations of motion, often called the SUVAT equations, describe the motion of objects moving with
. These five quantities and four equations form the foundation for solving most kinematics problems.

SUVAT stands for the five variables: s (displacement), u (initial velocity), v (final velocity), a (acceleration), and t (time). Each of the four equations connects four of these five variables, leaving one out.
Each equation connects four of the five variables. Choose the equation that contains the three known quantities and the one unknown you need to find.
Motion is in a straight line

Students often forget that SUVAT equations only work for constant acceleration. If an object speeds up then slows down, you must split the motion into separate phases, each with its own constant acceleration, and apply SUVAT to each phase separately.
"Use these equations for all motion problems"
— SUVAT only works for constant acceleration. Variable acceleration requires calculus or other methods.
— Deceleration is negative only if you've defined the direction of motion as positive.
— No! Velocity is zero, but acceleration due to gravity is still 10 m/s² downward.
"I can't solve it—I don't have enough information"
— You only need three of the five SUVAT variables to find the others.
— In these equations, yes. Negative time might arise algebraically but usually represents "before the start" and can be ignored.
